extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate/graduate students and teachers in mathematics and philosophy of mathematics (mathematical-methodology seminar)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and methodological criteria for producing and assessing mathematical conjectures, proofs, counterexamples, and definitions (as illustrated by the historical/problem-based dialogue about Euler's V - E + F = 2). Emphasis on thought-experiments, local vs global counterexamples, definitional disputes, and how to respond to refutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof as thought-experiment / quasi-experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'proof' may be a thought-experiment (a 'quasi-experiment') that suggests a decomposition of the original conjecture into subconjectures or lemmas, embedding it in a possibly different body of knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lakatos endorses treating certain proofs as heuristic thought-experiments (e.g., Cauchy's rubber-sheet triangulation proof): such proofs can be valuable even if they do not establish absolute truth. They show a strategy for proof by decomposing the main claim into lemmas, but each lemma must itself be scrutinized. Beware that embedding the problem in another theory (e.g., 'rubber-sheet' topology) introduces auxiliary assumptions needing justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decompose conjectures into explicit lemmas
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid proof-analysis decomposes the main conjecture into clear, explicit lemmas/subconjectures that together imply the main statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The teacher's proof of Euler's formula works by (1) removing a face and flattening, (2) triangulating, (3) removing triangles one-by-one; each step is a lemma. When producing or evaluating a proof, list the lemmas explicitly so each can be tested and potentially refuted by counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify every proof-step for all cases (avoid hidden assumptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every operation or step used in a proof (e.g., 'stretch the surface flat', 'triangulate', 'remove any triangle') must be justified to hold for the whole class of objects under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alpha, Beta, Gamma question steps 1–3 of the thought-experiment: you must show the flattening works for any polyhedron, triangulation yields new faces for every new edge, and triangle removal has only the claimed outcomes. Vague instructions like 'do it in any order' are insufficient; either prove existence of a suitable order or give a constructive method (example: show how to number triangles to preserve V-E+F).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish local vs global counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify counterexamples as 'local' (refuting a lemma or part of a proof but not the main conjecture) or 'global' (refuting the main conjecture itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gamma's example (removing an interior triangle) is a local counterexample to the third lemma but not to Euler's conjecture for the cube. Recognizing this distinction lets one decide whether to patch the proof (fix the lemma) or to abandon/modify the conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to local counterexamples by genuine lemma-improvement (local patching)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a counterexample only refutes a lemma, try to replace the false lemma by a stronger or more precise one which the counterexample does not refute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher modifies 'remove any triangle' to 'remove boundary triangles' and then further to 'remove triangles in an order that preserves V-E+F' — illustrating legitimate local patching. Such patches should be explicit and non-surreptitious; they must be checked for plausibility and for new vulnerabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat counterexamples with respect (do not dismiss them lightly)
rubrics_metrics.description: Counterexamples are decisive criticisms of conjectures or proofs and cannot be ignored; they should be used to refine theories or definitions rather than being casually dismissed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dialogue emphasizes that 'conjectures ignore dislike and suspicion, but they cannot ignore counterexamples.' Even 'monsters' may reveal important phenomena ('hopeful monsters').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ad hoc monster-barring (definitional exorcism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not respond to counterexamples by ad hoc redefinitions that exclude the counterexample solely to save the conjecture; this 'monster-barring' is methodologically suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delta's tactic of redefining 'polyhedron' to exclude nested cubes, stellated figures, picture-frames, or cylinders exemplifies monster-barring. The text warns that one can always save a conjecture by stipulative redefinition, but this sacrifices objectivity and may hide genuine mathematical problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agree on precise definitions / meanings before judging counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Objective criticism requires shared, explicit definitions (agreement on the extension of key terms) so that counterexamples are interpreted consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Much of the dispute arises because 'polyhedron', 'polygon', 'edge', 'face' are understood differently by participants; Lakatos recommends considering rival definitions and their consequences rather than secretly shifting meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make truth definitional (Def. P anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the tactic of redefining terms so that the desired theorem becomes true by definition (e.g., defining 'polyhedron' as 'object for which V-E+F=2').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alpha's suggestion to make Euler-ness definitional (Def. P) would eliminate substantive inquiry. Definitions should capture mathematical practice or conceptual content, not be engineered just to vindicate a conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit and honest about refinements to proofs ('I meant' is illegitimate)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof is repaired or a lemma strengthened, the change must be made explicitly and defended; retroactive 'I meant' reinterpretations are intellectually dishonest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher admits that saying 'I meant...' would be a surreptitious move; instead one should clearly state the new lemma/version and justify it. This preserves clarity and allows further genuine testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide constructive procedures or existence proofs for required operations
rubrics_metrics.description: If a proof requires performing a combinatorial or procedural task (e.g., ordering triangle removals), either provide an explicit construction or give a proof of existence of the required order/sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kappa asks how to construct the 'right order' of triangle removal; without such construction the thought-experiment 'proof' vanishes. Effective proofs should supply the means or an existence argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test conjectures broadly; corroboration by many examples is not proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical testing on many cases supports a conjecture but does not constitute proof; thorough checking can suggest proofs or reveal patterns but cannot substitute for rigorous justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euler and others had tested the formula on many classes (prisms, pyramids) and were confident, but Lakatos stresses that testing suggests proofs and conjectures but cannot replace them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pathological/edge cases (monsters) as probes for deeper understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Studying strange or pathological examples can expose hidden assumptions, lead to concept refinement, and advance theory; monsters may be 'hopeful' by revealing the need for new distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gamma defends studying lunatic fringe (star-polyhedra, picture-frame, cylinder) to learn about the heart of the subject. Lakatos argues that monsters shouldn't simply be exorcised; they often stimulate conceptual development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check applicability of auxiliary theories used in embeddings
rubrics_metrics.description: When a proof embeds the object into another theoretical framework (e.g., treating polyhedra as rubber sheets), verify that the auxiliary theory's assumptions apply to all intended cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The teacher's embedding of polyhedra into 'rubber sheets' introduces topological assumptions (e.g., homeomorphism to sphere) that fail for nested cubes or tunnels; always confirm the embedding is valid for the entire class.
